findings.headline: £1.000m waste infrastructure capital deferred to 2027/28 pending completion of strategic review
findings.detail: Council's Resource and Waste Strategy review, adopted in March 2024, remains ongoing with outline business case due end of 2026/27. Capital expenditure on waste services infrastructure has been deferred until 2027/28, resulting in a 47% underspend (£1.000m) on waste services budget projected for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Material deferral of strategic infrastructure investment; finance director needs revised capital programme timeline; lender needs visibility on when waste capacity decisions and expenditure will occur to assess council's service provision capacity.
findings.figures: Waste Services budget £2.128m, projected outturn £1.128m (underspend £1.000m, representing -47% variance)
findings.quote: The review is ongoing and aims to deliver the outline business case by the end of the 2026/27 financial year.

findings.headline: HRA financing costs forecast to rise 290 basis points due to capital programme expansion
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account financing costs (interest and MRP) forecast to increase from 16.4% of net revenue stream in 2025/26 to 19.3% in 2026/27, with further increase to 19.7% in 2027/28. Rise is driven by HRA capital expenditure expansion including WHQS improvements (£11.033m), major works (£3.150m), and SHARP programme (£4.841m) funded through borrowing. Financing costs then stabilize at 19.7% from 2028/29 onwards.
findings.matters: Material 290bp year-on-year increase puts HRA leverage approaching typical prudential limits. Lender needs to assess whether HRA revenue base can sustain these elevated financing costs long-term and whether HRA business model remains viable.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs 16.4% (2025/26 actual) rising to 19.3% (2026/27 forecast) and 19.7% (2027/28 estimate)
findings.quote: The increase in estimated CFR between 2025/26 and 2026/27 is estimated expenditure for the HRA and NEW Homes, Supported Borrowing, and Council Fund schemes including the Sustainable Communities for Schools programme and LGBI for Highways.

findings.headline: After over a decade of austerity, the council has exhausted most low-cost savings options and faces very difficult choices ahead
findings.detail: The council repeatedly emphasizes that the historic scale of cost reductions already taken across portfolios during austerity "leaves very limited options of scale for further cost reductions." Further reductions will require difficult choices with service impact.
findings.matters: This structural constraint means future budget gaps cannot be solved through incremental efficiency gains; they require material service cuts or tax increases
findings.figures: Over a decade of underfunding and cost reductions across all portfolios
findings.quote: As repeatedly reported, the scale of historic cost reductions already taken from portfolios during the period of austerity and beyond leaves very limited options of scale for further cost reductions and some very difficult choices will need to be made.

findings.headline: No official Welsh Government settlement for 2027/28 has been announced; budget planning is based on uncertain assumptions
findings.detail: The council is operating on three funding scenarios (pessimistic 1–2%, central 2–3%, optimistic 3–4% uplift) pending the official Welsh Government draft budget in mid-November. Each 1% uplift equals £2.940m. Current planning uses central case but carries material settlement risk.
findings.matters: Final budget position could shift materially once the settlement is known; worst-case scenario is 1% uplift delivering only £2.9m against a £27.9m requirement
findings.figures: 1% uplift = £2.940m; pessimistic scenario £2.940m–£5.880m; central £5.880m–£8.820m; optimistic £8.820m–£11.760m
findings.quote: At this stage, there is no official Welsh local government settlement for 2027/28 so all that we can do is base our assumptions on any potential implications from UK Spending Reviews and an assessment of the resulting outlook for the overall Welsh Government budget.

findings.headline: The council may not meet its statutory obligation to set a balanced budget by March 2027 if cost reductions prove insufficient
findings.detail: The document repeatedly warns that unless sufficient achievable and deliverable cost reductions are identified, the council will breach its statutory obligation to set a legal and balanced budget. This is stated as a direct risk, not a hypothetical.
findings.matters: Failure to set a balanced budget is a governance failure that could trigger Welsh Government intervention, external administration, or use of extraordinary powers
findings.figures: Legal budget deadline: March 2027
findings.quote: Unless sufficient cost reductions are identified that are achievable and deliverable the Council will not meet its statutory obligation to set a legal and balanced budget.

findings.headline: Of £10m in evaluated cost reductions across all portfolios, only £1.8m (18%) are rated low-risk; most carry high risk to service quality
findings.detail: When the council evaluated a 10% cost reduction exercise across portfolios, results were: Black (highest risk) £3.555m; Red £3.042m; Amber £1.597m; Green (lowest risk) £1.825m. The council explicitly notes it has proven "extremely difficult to identify areas that won't impact on service quality and standards."
findings.matters: Limited low-risk options means the council will be forced to implement high-risk cuts with direct impact on service provision, affecting both operational resilience and council income
findings.figures: Green (low-risk): £1.825m; Amber: £1.597m; Red: £3.042m; Black (highest-risk): £3.555m; total £10.019m
findings.quote: As expected, it has proven extremely difficult to identify areas that won't impact on service quality and standards.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 balanced budget relied on non-recurring Welsh Government funding and pension contribution relief that will not repeat
findings.detail: Last year the council benefited from a late Welsh Government budget agreement and a significant positive contribution from a triennial pension actuarial review. Both are explicitly described as unlikely to be available again, meaning 2027/28 cannot rely on these tailwinds.
findings.matters: This explains why the 2027/28 position is materially worse despite similar stated budget pressures, and shows the previous year's balance was not structural
findings.figures: 2026/27 benefited from 4.5% uplift following additional negotiations
findings.quote: This greatly assisted with enabling the Council to set a legal and balanced budget for the 2026/27 financial year and is unlikely to be available again.

findings.headline: The council is projecting a significant overspend in 2026/27 and plans to draw down earmarked reserves to cover it
findings.detail: The document states that due to a projected overspend in the current financial year, the council will release available earmarked reserves to improve the in-year position. It warns that using reserves to balance the budget should only occur for one-off or time-limited costs, not for structural deficits.
findings.matters: Using reserves to cover operational deficits in the current year signals worsening cash position and reduces the buffer available for future shocks
findings.figures: No specific reserve figure disclosed; draws occurring in 2026/27
findings.quote: Due to the significant projected overspend in the current financial year, any earmarked reserves that can be released will be required to improve the in-year position.

findings.headline: The council faces a £19–22m structural budget gap for 2027/28 under central funding assumptions
findings.detail: Flintshire identified an additional budget requirement of £27.866m for 2027/28. Under central planning assumptions (2–3% funding uplift from Welsh Government), this leaves a shortfall of £19.046m to £21.986m. Even under optimistic scenarios (3–4% uplift), the gap remains £16–19m. The council must find solutions through cost reductions and increased income to set a legal and balanced budget.
findings.matters: A structural gap of this magnitude indicates the council cannot sustain current service levels without major reductions; it signals material pressure on financial sustainability for a borrower
findings.figures: £27.866m additional budget requirement; £19.046m–£21.986m shortfall (central scenario); £16.106m–£19.046m shortfall (optimistic scenario)
findings.quote: If the analysis above is an accurate reflection of the likely Welsh Government settlement, the Council would still need to identify a combination of additional income (including local taxation) and cost reductions in the region of £19.046m to £21.986m based on the central planning assumption.

findings.headline: Reserves rated Amber (score 9), flagged as a material risk requiring mitigation
findings.detail: The council classifies reserve adequacy as an Amber risk at 9 out of 25, indicating it judges reserves insufficient for its identified risks. The score has not changed from the previous quarter.
findings.matters: Reserves function as the council's financial buffer against revenue shocks; an Amber rating signals limited financial flexibility in a period of MTFS and schools stress.
findings.figures: Risk Score 9 out of 25
findings.quote: RCF01 – Reserves – Risk Score 9 (Same, previously 9)

findings.headline: Financial viability of schools is rated Red at score 25, the highest risk on the corporate register
findings.detail: Schools financial viability is the single highest-rated risk at 25 out of 25 and has not improved. Schools represent a material delegated budget; financial distress there cascades into council-wide sustainability issues and borrowing requirements.
findings.matters: Schools absorb a large share of council spending; financial difficulties in delegated budgets force the council into additional spending or borrowing.
findings.figures: Risk Score 25 out of 25; highest risk on register
findings.quote: REY01 - Financial Viability of Schools – Risk Score 25 (Same, previously 25)

findings.headline: Medium-term Financial Strategy rated Red (score 20 out of 25), unchanged from previous quarter
findings.detail: The MTFS remains at the council's second-highest risk level with no improvement made. This indicates material challenges in the council's ability to balance its budget over the medium term, a core concern for service continuity.
findings.matters: A lender requires confidence in the council's three-to-five-year budget sustainability; a Red MTFS rating signals structural imbalance requiring resolution.
findings.figures: Risk Score 20 out of 25
findings.quote: RCF18 - Medium-term Financial Strategy (MTFS) – Risk Score 20 (Same, previously 20)

findings.headline: Strategic Transformation Programme £2m savings target carries 'significant identified risk' with business cases due October
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes a £2m cost reduction target from the Strategic Transformation Programme, 'currently assumed to be met in full.' Cabinet approved new projects in June now at detailed business case stage, 'due to be completed in October.' This will provide 'a more accurate assessment of the likely cost reduction achievable compared with the target.' The risk is that October may reveal a shortfall.
findings.matters: The council has assumed £2m of savings that depend on business cases not yet completed. At Month 4, this is a major budget assumption still entirely unvalidated. If October reveals slippage, the council will need emergency mitigations.
findings.figures: £2m savings target; business cases due October 2026
findings.quote: A cost reduction target of £2m has been included in the budget which was based on a combination of existing and new projects planned for commencement in 2026/27 and is currently assumed to be met in full. Cabinet approved some new projects in June which are now being progressed to detailed business case stage and are due to be completed in October.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection down 0.4% year-on-year with service vacancies affecting recovery
findings.detail: Council Tax collection rates are 0.4% lower than the same point last year (37.6% vs 38.0% at end July). The shortfall is 'primarily due to effects of new regulations governing recovery action' and an extended pre-court period before enforcement action. The service is 'currently operating with several vacancies, which has placed further pressure on recovery activity.'
findings.matters: Collection is declining due to regulatory constraint and staffing shortage, not resident behaviour alone. This is structural: the new recovery regulations are not changing mid-year. Vacancy-driven shortfalls compound the collection pressure.
findings.figures: Collection at end July 37.6% vs 38.0% prior year; shortfall 0.4 percentage points
findings.quote: Council tax collection rates for 2026/27 are currently 0.4% lower than the equivalent point last year (collections at the end of July are 37.6% compared to 38.0% in the previous year). This is primarily due to effects of new regulations governing recovery action

findings.headline: Welsh Government waste recycling infraction penalty of £1.022m pending outcome of September meeting
findings.detail: The authority did not meet the 70% statutory recycling target in 2024/25 and faces a potential infraction fine of £1,022,386. Welsh Government previously waived £1.203m in infraction charges for 2021/22–2023/24. Officers are meeting with the Cabinet Minister in September 2026 to discuss progress and this 'will assist with determining the levying of the infraction charge.'
findings.matters: This is a contingent penalty that may or may not be levied within the financial year. If levied, it is a material one-off charge to reserves. The outcome is determined outside the council's control and is imminent.
findings.figures: Potential infraction fine £1,022,386; prior waived fines £1.203m; decision meeting September 2026
findings.quote: However, the authority did not meet the increased statutory recycling target of 70% in 2024/25, which means that a further infraction fine of £1,022,386 could be levied

findings.headline: Holiday pay tribunal claims (Harpur Trust v Brazel) carry contingent liability risk beyond £0.254m reserve
findings.detail: The Supreme Court upheld the Harpur Trust v Brazel judgment in July 2022, affecting holiday pay calculations for irregular-hours and term-time staff. Flintshire has 300+ live employment claims in tribunal. The council holds £0.254m in reserves but 'there is a risk that the final cost may be considerably more.' Case management orders extend to January 2027.
findings.matters: This is a known contingent liability with a court-determined principle but uncertain quantum. The reserve held (£0.254m) may significantly understate eventual cost. This is an unfunded legacy liability.
findings.figures: 300+ live employment tribunal claims; £0.254m reserve held; decisions pending to January 2027
findings.quote: There are currently 300+ live employment claims progressing through the employment tribunal. There is a risk that the final cost may be considerably more than the £0.254m currently held in reserves for this purpose.

findings.headline: Pay award inflation of 3.3% for NJC (Green Book) staff against 3% budget creates £0.281m shortfall
findings.detail: The budget assumed a 3% pay award for NJC (Green Book) staff from April 2026. The national employers' pay offer of 3.3% was just agreed. The council has identified an in-year shortfall of around £0.281m that 'may need to be met from reserves if there is no compensatory grant allocation.'
findings.matters: This is one of many pay pressures. Welsh Government is consulting on a 3.5% teacher award (vs 3% budgeted) and a 5% increase for unqualified teachers. Pay modelling has a £1m budget for recruitment/retention reform. The council faces both catch-up and structural pay cost issues.
findings.figures: NJC shortfall £0.281m; budgeted teacher award 3%, WG consulting on 3.5%
findings.quote: It is estimated that there will be an in-year shortfall to the budget of around £0.281m that may need to be met from reserves if there is no compensatory grant allocation.

findings.headline: School sector holding cumulative deficit reserves of £4.798m, adverse movement of £4.199m in one year
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, schools held reserves in deficit totalling £4.798m, an adverse movement of £4.199m from the prior year. The council holds a centrally-held non-delegated exit costs budget to meet redundancy costs for schools, and there is 'a significant risk that the approved budget is exceeded as specific schools work through any required redundancy processes.'
findings.matters: School deficits are a structural problem moving fast. A £4.2m deterioration in one year suggests either falling pupil numbers or cost pressures schools cannot absorb. Redundancy costs are a lagging indicator of deeper stress.
findings.figures: School earmarked reserves deficit £4.798m at 31 March 2026; adverse movement of £4.199m from 31 March 2025
findings.quote: In recent years there has been considerable pressure on school delegated budgets with school earmarked reserves held on 31 March 2026 equating to an overall deficit position of (£4.798m), an adverse movement of (£4.199m) from 31 March 2025

findings.headline: Streetscene & Transportation overspend of £1.739m driven by income shortfalls and waste disposal cost volatility
findings.detail: S&T is £1.739m over budget. Key pressures: HRC trade waste income down £0.200m due to lack of business take-up; DIY household waste income down £0.285m following member decision not to implement full charging; waste disposal costs up £0.520m for wood, hazardous waste, and bulky items. Income targets are not being achieved and disposal costs are volatile.
findings.matters: Traded service income shortfalls and volatile waste procurement costs are both controllable in theory but the council has not controlled them. The DIY waste pressure persists despite being a known prior-year issue.
findings.figures: Total S&T overspend £1.739m; HRC trade waste shortfall £0.200m; DIY waste shortfall £0.285m; waste disposal pressures £0.520m
findings.quote: There is a projected shortfall of £0.200m for Household Recycling Centre (HRC) trade waste income due to lack of take-up from businesses and a further £0.285m shortfall for the underachievement of the DIY household waste income target.

findings.headline: Contingency reserves will fall to £2.187m after overspend, down from £5.072m opening
findings.detail: Opening contingency balance was £5.072m. After taking account of approved allocations and the projected £4.386m overspend (net of risk reserve), the closing balance is forecast at £2.187m. Base level reserves are £8.985m, so unearmarked reserves overall fall from £18.261m to £11.172m.
findings.matters: Falling reserves flag two concerns: whether the overspend is a one-year event or structural, and whether the council has headroom for further unforeseen pressure. A council using 40% of unearmarked reserves in one year is under stress.
findings.figures: Opening contingency £5.072m; closing contingency £2.187m; total unearmarked reserves move from £18.261m to £11.172m
findings.quote: A projected contingency reserve balance as at 31st March 2027 of £2.187m (after taking account of previously approved allocations including those approved as part of the 2026/27 Budget).

findings.headline: Out of County Placements overspend by £1.685m with explicit forecast of further increases
findings.detail: The pooled budget for children's and education out-of-county placements is £1.685m over approved budget. The report is explicit: 'there is a significant risk that the projected overspend will continue to increase during the year' as new high-cost placements are added. The budget included an additional £2m but spend is already exceeding it.
findings.matters: This is a known-bad forecast at Month 4. If the council was £1.7m over on a budget that had already absorbed an extra £2m in the plan, the outturn risk to year-end is material.
findings.figures: £1.685m overspend; budget included £2m additional provision; current caseload-only forecast excludes contingency for new placements
findings.quote: Several new high-cost placements have been added to the current cohort in the early part of the financial year causing projected expenditure to exceed the approved budget. The projected overspend is based on the current caseload of placements and excludes any contingency for net new placements. Therefore, there is a significant risk that the projected overspend will continue to increase during the year.

findings.headline: Social Services demand-led overspend of £4.390m with no control mechanism visible
findings.detail: Social Services (excluding Out of County) is £4.390m over budget at Month 4. Adult social care packages show £2.194m overspend for Learning Disability independently-provided services and £0.520m for Physical Disability services. Children's Services is £1.056m over due to agency staffing for social workers. The action plan promises reviews and efficiency but no hard savings.
findings.matters: Social care demand and unit costs are structural. If a council cannot hold spend at Month 4 when placements are known, the risk that the £4m settles lower is low. Unit costs (per placement) matter for sustainability.
findings.figures: Social Services £4.390m; Learning Disability packages £2.194m; PDSI services £0.520m; agency staff costs £0.772m
findings.quote: The costs of care packages for independently provided services for the Learning Disability service are resulting in an overspend of £2.194m which includes care provision through direct payments, supported living and residential services.

findings.headline: Projected £7.090m operating deficit requiring urgent action
findings.detail: The Council faces an operating deficit of £7.090m (reducing to £4.386m with use of Budget Risk Reserve). The report states this is 'clearly of significant concern and needs to be addressed urgently to bring expenditure back in line with the approved budget.' This is not a small variance but 1.7% of total budget.
findings.matters: A deficit of this magnitude signals either structural cost pressures the council cannot control or demand-led services that have broken their budgets midyear; either is a lender concern.
findings.figures: £7.090m deficit; £4.386m after budget risk reserve utilisation; approved budget £421.860m
findings.quote: An operating deficit of £7.090m (this reduces to £4.386 with the full utilisation of the remaining £2.704m budget risk reserve).

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Strategic Transformation Programme targets £2m of cost reductions but progress to date is unreported
findings.detail: The council has a Strategic Transformation Programme with a £2m cost reduction target in the 2026/27 budget and is continuing to add new projects. However, the document states only that 'work is underway to assess the progress' with no detail on whether the £2m target has been met or is on track to delivery.
findings.matters: If the Strategic Transformation Programme does not deliver its £2m target, the council will face an even larger funding gap in 2027/28. Vague progress reporting suggests there may be implementation challenges.
findings.figures: £2m cost reduction target in 2026/27
findings.quote: Work is underway to assess the progress of the various projects and to identify any cost reductions that can be factored into the estimates.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Council reserves remain relatively low compared to other Welsh councils
findings.detail: Whilst the council's reserves position improved in 2025/26, the council explicitly states that reserves 'still remain relatively low in comparison to many Welsh Councils'. This limits the council's ability to absorb overspends or unfunded pressures without borrowing.
findings.matters: Lower reserves reduce financial resilience. If the council faces unexpected demand spikes (in Out of County Placements or Homelessness) or pay costs exceed budget, it has limited liquidity to cover shortfalls without further borrowing.
findings.figures: Reserves improved but relatively low compared to Welsh Council peers
findings.quote: The improved 2025/26 year end position has resulted in the council holding a higher level of reserves than anticipated although they still remain relatively low in comparison to many Welsh Councils.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Streetscene grant funding has already been significantly reduced in 2026/27 with further cuts to key funding streams at risk
findings.detail: The council reports that DEFRA (pEPR) funding 'has been subject to a significant reduction in 2026/27' and identifies 'significant risks' of further reductions in both Sustainable Waste Management Grant and DEFRA funding for the future. This represents loss of income that cannot easily be recovered through service charges.
findings.matters: Grant-funded services that lose income cannot simply cut services without incurring statutory liabilities or social pressure. Loss of waste management grant funding would force either service cuts or council tax increases to maintain services.
findings.figures: DEFRA funding already subject to significant reduction in 2026/27
findings.quote: There are also significant risks within the portfolio in relation to potential grant reductions for Sustainable Waste Management Grant and DEFRA (pEPR) funding which has been subject to a significant reduction in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Homelessness demand is growing significantly but no additional budget has been included for 2027/28
findings.detail: The council reports 'significant growth' in numbers presenting as homeless and needing temporary accommodation. Despite this observed trend, the council has explicitly stated no increase is being included for 2027/28. The council acknowledges demand levels 'are difficult to predict so will need to be kept under close review throughout this financial year'.
findings.matters: Growing demand without corresponding budget provision creates risk of mid-year overspends. As a statutory obligation, the council must accommodate homeless persons regardless of budget, meaning any overspend would draw on reserves or force cuts elsewhere.
findings.figures: Significant growth noted; no provision for 2027/28
findings.quote: There also continues to be a significant growth in numbers presenting as homeless and needing to be accommodated within temporary accommodation... No increase is included at this stage for 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Social Care demand pressures of £6.509m, the largest single budget increase, driven by inflation and service demand growth
findings.detail: Social care accounts for £6.509m of the total £27.759m budget requirement, covering commissioned care, transition to adulthood, domiciliary care/reablement, children's residential care and carers direct payments. The council states the impact of inflation and increasing service demands 'continues to be challenging' but provides no assurance these pressures are fully funded.
findings.matters: Social care is a statutory service where unmet demand creates fallback liability on the council. Escalating costs from both inflation and demand suggest this area is vulnerable to mid-year overspends.
findings.figures: Social Care £6.509m (second largest pressure after £8.474m pay)
findings.quote: The impact of inflation and increases in service demands continues to be challenging. The cost pressures identified to date include commissioned care, transition to adulthood, domiciliary care/reablement, children's residential care and carers direct payments.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Out of County Placements continues to grow unpredictably with £2m added to both 2026/27 and 2027/28 budgets
findings.detail: The council added £2m to Out of County Placements in the 2026/27 budget and is adding a further £2m for 2027/28. However, the council acknowledges 'high volatility in this area' and that 'it is very difficult to project future demand levels'. The consecutive-year additions suggest ongoing escalation that may not yet be fully captured.
findings.matters: Volatile, unpredictable demand in Out of County Placements (typically children's residential placements and high-cost case work) poses significant cost overrun risk. If actual demand exceeds the £2m addition, the council will face mid-year overspends and deeper budget pressure.
findings.figures: £2m additional for 2026/27; £2m additional for 2027/28
findings.quote: Due to the high volatility in this area it is very difficult to project future demand levels at this early stage of the year. At this stage, a further additional amount of £2m has been included which will be subject to review over the coming months.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Trade unions have rejected the latest pay offer and are balloting for industrial action
findings.detail: The NJC (Green Book) pay offer for 2026/27 of 3.2% has been rejected by trade union members who are currently being balloted for potential industrial action. The council has budgeted 3% for 2027/28 but any final award higher than current offers will require adjustment to the budget, adding cost pressure on top of the existing shortfall.
findings.matters: Industrial action poses an immediate financial risk if final pay settlements exceed budget assumptions. The council already has £8.474m budgeted for pay awards; further increases would deepen the funding gap.
findings.figures: Pay awards £8.474m budgeted for 2027/28; current offer rejected at 3.2%
findings.quote: The latest pay offer for the current year (2026/27) has been rejected and Trade Union Members are currently being balloted for potential industrial action.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: £27.759m unfunded budget gap for 2027/28 with no Welsh Government funding settlement yet confirmed
findings.detail: The council faces an additional budget requirement of £27.759m for the coming year, an increase from the £26.578m initially projected. Welsh Government has provided no indicative figures for the Aggregate External Finance (AEF) that funds 70% of the council's budget, making financial planning extremely uncertain. Each 1% uplift in AEF equates to £2.94m, so without new funding the council will need to find savings equivalent to a service cut or significant council tax rise.
findings.matters: An unfunded structural deficit threatens the council's financial sustainability and ability to service debt. Lenders will be concerned about forced service reductions or whether the council can balance its budget.
findings.figures: £27.759m budget requirement; AEF provides ~70% of funding; each 1% AEF uplift = £2.94m
findings.quote: the Council clearly has another serious and major budget challenge for the financial year 2027/28 if there is no movement in national funding expectations which is woefully insufficient to the level required to meet current service demand and inflationary impacts

findings.headline: Council has allocated £248k to mitigate inflationary pressures on capital schemes
findings.detail: A specific provision was made to offset potential cost inflation on current capital schemes given current economic conditions. The council expects capital project costs may rise during 2026/27.
findings.matters: Signals the council's concern about construction cost inflation and lack of confidence that budgeted amounts will be sufficient.
findings.figures: £0.248m inflation provision
findings.quote: Inflationary pressures - £0.248m. Request to set funding aside to mitigate potential pressures of current schemes within the capital programme given the economic climate.

findings.headline: Holywell Bank project funding is contingent on securing Welsh Government grant
findings.detail: A £447k capital allocation for the former HSBC Bank purchase (to be repurposed for retail and transitional housing) is dependent on approval of a Welsh Government Circular Economy grant application. If the grant is not approved, the allocation is to be returned to the capital programme.
findings.matters: The project viability depends entirely on external grant approval; if declined, the council will need to reprioritise capital resources or scale back the scheme.
findings.figures: £0.447m contingent allocation
findings.quote: A Circular Economy grant bid for this funding will be submitted to WG and if successful, this allocation will be returned to the capital programme.

findings.headline: Council Fund underspend more than doubled year-on-year with no explanation
findings.detail: Council Fund spending fell from 97.60% of budget in 2024/25 to 94% in 2025/26, creating a £2.811m carry forward. The paper states this reflects 'reviewed spending plans' but provides no explanation for the significant increase in underspend or whether schemes are behind schedule.
findings.matters: A doubling of underspend could indicate capital projects are falling behind schedule, which lenders need to understand if it signals delivery or planning issues.
findings.quote: This shows that 96.25% of the budget has been spent (CF 94.00%, HRA 100%). Corresponding figures for Outturn 2024/25 were 98.23% (CF 97.60%, HRA 100%).

findings.headline: Funding surplus improved by £420k more than forecast
findings.detail: The capital programme ended with a £4.508m surplus for 2025/26-2027/28, exceeding the £4.088m projected when the 2026/27-2028/29 programme was approved in December 2025. This suggests better than expected capital funding or lower spend than anticipated.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council's capital position is more resilient than initially forecast, giving lenders confidence in financial management.
findings.figures: £4.508m outturn surplus vs £4.088m forecast (£0.420m improvement)
findings.quote: This provides a final outturn funding surplus from the 2025/26 – 2027/28 Capital Programme of £4.508m which is £0.420m more than the projected £4.088m when the 2026/27 – 2028/29 Capital Programme was approved on the 3 December 2025.

findings.headline: Fleet ultra-low emission vehicle transition delayed due to infrastructure deficit and deferred to 2026/27
findings.detail: A £0.680m carry-forward for fleet ULEV transition has been deferred because the council 'currently does not have the grid capacity at its depot in Alltami to provide electric vehicle charging without significant investment'. An options appraisal was completed with external support but requires 'a preferred option and develop the business case for how the Council will proceed with its depot assets'. The original plan was a phased transition between 2024 and 2030 with an additional £2m approved in 2024/25.
findings.matters: The council has identified a capital infrastructure constraint (depot grid capacity) that blocks planned fleet modernisation. This suggests capital planning did not anticipate operational constraints, and 'significant investment' is now needed. The deferral pushes costs forward and the business case is incomplete.
findings.figures: £0.680m carry forward; original £2m approved for 2024/25; planned transition 2024-2030
findings.quote: There has been a delayed transition to ultra-low emission vehicles (ULEVs) as the Council currently does not have the grid capacity at its depot in Alltami to provide electric vehicle charging without significant investment.

findings.headline: New recurring ICT costs of £0.187m per annum committed for contact centre and telephony replacement
findings.detail: A carry-forward of £0.480m is being transferred to the Digital Strategy Reserve to fund replacement of telephony and contact centre solutions. The council projects an upfront investment of £0.080m plus an ongoing annual increase of £0.187m per annum 'on top of the existing revenue budget', with the carry-forward expected to fund this for 2 years to 31 March 2029. Funding beyond that date 'would require inclusion in the Council's Medium Term Financial Strategy'.
findings.matters: The council is committing to new recurring costs at a time when the MTFS outlook is already flagged as challenging. An additional £0.187m annual commitment reduces future budget flexibility. The fact that funding beyond 2029 is unresolved is a budget pressure point.
findings.figures: £0.480m carry forward; £0.080m upfront investment; £0.187m per annum increase from current baseline
findings.quote: It is estimated that the replacement technology for the telephony solution and contact centre will require £0.080m upfront investment with an annual increase of £0.187m per annum on top of the existing revenue budget that funds the current technologies.

findings.headline: Medium-term outlook beyond 2026/27 flagged as challenging with urgent need for early budget planning
findings.detail: The report includes explicit forward warning that the outlook for 2027/28 and beyond 'remains challenging' and calls for 'prioritisation needs to be given to early budget planning over the coming months'. This signals the council's finance team expects deteriorating position in the medium term, requiring urgent action.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need forward visibility. A council flagging its own medium-term challenges suggests budget pressures are known and materialising. The fact this warning appears in the outturn (not just budget planning papers) elevates concern.
findings.figures: No specific figures; this is a qualitative forward warning
findings.quote: Looking beyond 2026/27, the outlook for 2027/28 and beyond remains challenging and prioritisation needs to be given to early budget planning over the coming months

findings.headline: Spending moratorium and vacancy controls must continue into 2026/27 to maintain budget balance
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that the moratorium on non-contractually committed spend and vacancy management process introduced in 2023/24 will continue throughout 2025/26 and 'will need to carry on into 2026/27'. The positive £3.566m movement from Month 10 was driven by continued 'review and challenge of non-essential spend and vacancy controls', not by structural improvement.
findings.matters: A council relying on vacancy freezes and spending moratoriums to balance budget is managing through constraint, not structural improvement. This becomes unsustainable in a growing service area and indicates the underlying budget does not cover current service demand.
findings.figures: £3.566m positive movement from Month 10 attributed to 'continuation of review and challenge of non-essential spend and vacancy controls'
findings.quote: The moratorium on non-contractually committed spend and vacancy management process put in place during 2023/24 continued throughout 2025/26 and will need to carry on into 2026/27.

findings.headline: Social Services overspending persistently, with out-of-county placements driving £2.573m overrun
findings.detail: Social Services exceeded budget by £4.613m (budget £104.2m, actual £108.812m). Within this, Out of County Placements overspent by £2.573m against a £22.621m budget. While the portfolio improved by £1.312m from Month 10 projections, the overall overspend reflects structural cost pressures in residential placements, particularly for children's services where new placements were cited as a key driver.
findings.matters: A persistent 4.4% overspend in the council's largest service area suggests demographic or commissioning pressures that will recur. Out-of-county placement costs are difficult to control and typically grow with demand.
findings.figures: Social Services £4.613m overspend; Out of County Placements £2.573m overspend (10.4% of budget); Month 10 deficit of £2.776m improved by £3.566m but overspend remains entrenched
findings.quote: Out of County - £0.708m Children's Services – due to a number of new placements £0.725m

findings.headline: Reserves flagged as amber-level risk with no detail on the underlying issue
findings.detail: Reserves hold an amber risk score of 9, unchanged from the prior quarter. The paper does not disclose the actual reserve balance, reserve policy, adequacy ratios, or what specifically is driving the risk assessment.
findings.matters: Reserve levels and reserve adequacy are key indicators of financial flexibility and resilience; a lender needs to understand the reserve position and why reserves are flagged as a risk.
findings.figures: Risk score 9, unchanged
findings.quote: RCF01 – Reserves – Risk Score 9 (Same, previously 9)

findings.headline: Medium-term Financial Strategy remains at high risk (score 20) with no improvement
findings.detail: MTFS holds a red-level risk score of 20, unchanged from the previous quarter, making it joint-highest with school viability. This persistent high-risk rating on the council's multi-year financial plan suggests unresolved structural issues, but the paper provides no detail on drivers or mitigation actions.
findings.matters: A council's medium-term financial strategy is foundational to financial sustainability. Persistent high risk on the MTFS indicates structural budget challenges have not been resolved and may worsen.
findings.figures: Risk score 20, unchanged from prior quarter
findings.quote: RCF18 - Medium-term Financial Strategy (MTFS) – Risk Score 20 (Same, previously 20)

findings.headline: School financial viability risk deteriorated to 25, now the highest-rated corporate risk
findings.detail: School financial viability (REY01) is the only risk that worsened in the quarter ending 31st March 2026, rising from score 20 to 25. It is now the joint-highest risk on the register. The paper does not explain what is driving the deterioration or describe mitigation actions.
findings.matters: Schools are a significant statutory obligation and major cost centre for councils. Deteriorating financial viability signals emerging cash flow pressures or rising costs that may require unplanned council subsidy or threaten service delivery.
findings.figures: Risk score 25 (up from 20)
findings.quote: REY01 - Financial Viability of Schools – Risk Score 25 (Deteriorated, previously 20)

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, Treasury Management Policy Statement, Practices and Schedules 2026-2029.
findings.headline: Budget sensitivity to interest rate assumptions: 5.4% borrowing and 3.58% investment return depend on volatile market conditions
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget for interest costs assumes £15.6m on long-term borrowing at an average rate of 4.53%, and £1.27m investment income on a £35.5m portfolio at 3.58%. The interest rate forecast acknowledges 'continued volatility' and short-term fluctuations from economic data and geopolitical developments. The council explicitly warns that if actual rates diverge from forecasts, budget performance will correspondingly worsen.
findings.matters: A council in rising leverage positions is more sensitive to rate changes. If long-term rates remain above the 5.4% new-borrowing assumption, debt service costs will exceed budget and force reserves or services downward.
findings.figures: Interest budget 2026/27: £15.6m on long-term loans; investment income budget £1.27m; rates forecast include 'continued volatility'
findings.quote: If levels of investments, borrowing and interest rates differ from those forecast, performance against budget will be correspondingly different.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, Treasury Management Policy Statement, Practices and Schedules 2026-2029.
findings.headline: Usable reserves falling 24% from £79m to £60m as earmarked funds are spent, reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: The council's usable reserves are declining from £79m in 2024/25 to £60m by 2028/29. This fall is explicitly attributed to earmarked reserves being drawn down as their designated purposes fall due for payment. With capital programmes expanding and reserves depleting in tandem, the council has less liquidity buffer for unexpected costs or revenue pressures.
findings.matters: Reserves are the primary buffer against cash flow shocks. A 24% reduction over four years, combined with rising borrowing needs, indicates tightening financial resilience.
findings.figures: Usable reserves: £79m (2024/25) declining to £60m (2028/29)
findings.quote: The level of reserves the Council has is expected to fall in 2025/26 as funding earmarked for specific purposes falls due for payment.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, Treasury Management Policy Statement, Practices and Schedules 2026-2029.
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement rising £68m to £433m by 2028/29, with borrowing need climbing to £135m
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need (Capital Financing Requirement) is forecast to increase from £365m currently to £433m by 2028/29. This is driven by large capital schemes: schools (Sustainable Communities for Learning programme), children's residential care, and HRA social housing building. Simultaneously, usable reserves are falling from £79m to £60m, creating a structural shift from internal borrowing toward sustained external finance. By 2028/29, the council will need to raise £135m in new borrowing.
findings.matters: This represents rising leverage and a structural change in the council's financing position. It signals increased debt service costs and reduced financial flexibility to absorb pressures.
findings.figures: CFR: £365m (2024/25) to £433m (2028/29); borrowing required: £135m by 2028/29
findings.quote: Table 3 shows the Council's CFR increases during 2026/27, this is linked with the capital programme (examples of schemes funded by borrowing include the Sustainable Communities for Learning schools programme, development of children's residential care and the HRA capital programme, which includes building new social housing). The combination of the increase in capital expenditure and a reduction in reserves, results in a sustained requirement for new borrowing over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, Treasury Management Policy Statement, Practices and Schedules 2026-2029.
findings.headline: £18.95m of LOBO loans face interest rate resets in 2026/27, likely to trigger refinancing at higher cost
findings.detail: Flintshire holds £18.95m of LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where lenders can propose rate increases at set dates. All of these loans have reset options falling during 2026/27. With long-term interest rates now higher than when the loans were originated, the council expects lenders to exercise these options, forcing the council to refinance at current market rates rather than accept higher rates.
findings.matters: This is a known, near-term cash flow obligation that will increase debt service costs. It represents identifiable refinancing risk on a material sum.
findings.figures: £18.95m in LOBO loans with all options during 2026/27
findings.quote: All of these LOBOs have options during 2026/27, and with long-term interest rates having risen in recent years, there is now a good chance that lenders will exercise their options. If they do, the Council will take the option to repay LOBO loans to reduce refinancing risk in later years.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: Pay award assumptions of 3% carry execution risk; if national agreements exceed this, the difference must be met from the Contingency Reserve
findings.detail: The budget assumes a 3% pay award for teaching and non-teaching staff from April 2026. The council notes: 'However, in the absence of additional funding, should national pay agreements conclude at a higher level, the difference may need to be met from the Contingency Reserve.' While Welsh Government provided additional funding in 2025/26 for pay additionality, no such provision is guaranteed for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A 1% pay award overage (if agreed at 4% instead of 3%) would cost approximately £0.8-1m and would need to come from contingency reserves, which are already thin at £2.906m.
findings.figures: 3% assumption; contingency reserve £2.906m
findings.quote: However, in the absence of additional funding, should national pay agreements conclude at a higher level, the difference may need to be met from the Contingency Reserve.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: Homelessness demand is increasing and 'difficult to predict', with mitigation being delivered through temporary grant funding and asset borrowing
findings.detail: The council faced an additional £4.5m for homelessness in 2025/26 and notes: 'Demand levels are still increasing however we are currently able to offset the increased costs of Bed and Breakfast by using additional properties from the Housing Revenue Account (HRA), D2 PropCo and the purchase of properties utilising Welsh Government Transitional Accommodation Capital Programme (TACP) funding.' The paper cautions: 'Demand levels in the future will be difficult to predict so will need to be kept under close review as we move into 2026/27.' The mitigation relies on Welsh Government grants and HRA liquidity, which are not guaranteed.
findings.matters: Homelessness demand is growing and unpredictable. The current mitigation strategy relies on temporary Welsh Government grants and asset borrowing from the HRA, both of which could be withdrawn or constrained, leaving the council exposed to demand it cannot control.
findings.figures: £4.5m added to 2025/26 budget; demand levels 'still increasing'
findings.quote: Demand levels are still increasing however we are currently able to offset the increased costs of Bed and Breakfast by using additional properties from the Housing Revenue Account (HRA), D2 PropCo and the purchase of properties utilising Welsh Government Transitional Accommodation Capital Programme (TACP) funding.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: The medium-term financial forecast shows £26.5m+ additional budget requirement in both 2027/28 and 2028/29, with no indicative allocations from Welsh Government
findings.detail: Table 7 projects cumulative additional budget requirements of £26.578m (2027/28) and £26.580m (2028/29), driven primarily by pay inflation (£8.3-8.5m per year) and social care pressures (£7.9-10m per year). Critically, the paper notes: 'The 2026/27 Final Settlement excluded an indicative all-Wales revenue allocation for 2027/28 which will continue to make our financial planning arrangements challenging.' This creates visibility of major funding gaps but no clarity on funding solutions.
findings.matters: The council can see a £26.5m+ problem in each of the next two years but has no forward funding allocation from Welsh Government to meet it. This signals that the council will need to identify additional cost reductions or increases to tax/borrowing, but has limited room to do so.
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Final Settlement excluded an indicative all-Wales revenue allocation for 2027/28 which will continue to make our financial planning arrangements challenging.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: The Chief Executive explicitly states the council's financial position is 'increasingly precarious' and there are 'no longer any cost reductions of scale'
findings.detail: In the Chief Executive's formal advice (para 1.42), they state: 'Quite simply there are no longer any cost reductions of scale, and the councils financial position will become increasingly precarious.' They also note that the council remains 'an underfunded Council' and that the improved settlement 'does not address the financial challenges the Council continues to face.' The Chief Executive expresses specific concern about 'Social Services, Streetscene Services and Education particularly' as demand-led services that are 'currently exposed to a number of demand led pressures which are challenging to manage and often difficult to predict.'
findings.matters: The Chief Executive is explicitly warning that cost reduction options have been exhausted and the council is entering a precarious position. This is a material governance and financial stability warning from the council's most senior officer.
findings.figures: No specific figures, but covers all three largest demand-led services
findings.quote: Quite simply there are no longer any cost reductions of scale, and the councils financial position will become increasingly precarious.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves are projected to collapse from £5.957m to £2.068m by end of 2026/27, alongside a cumulative schools budget deficit
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves (those ring-fenced for specific purposes) are forecast to fall by 65% from £5.957m to £2.068m. Additionally, schools are projected to have a cumulative net deficit position of £5.233m by end of 2026/27 (see Appendix 8). The paper notes: 'School balances have fallen year-on-year for a number of years and this downward trend is likely to continue.' This represents structural deterioration in the schools funding position.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves and falling school balances signal that the council is consuming its financial buffers and that schools are moving towards structural deficit. This is unsustainable and will require intervention.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves: £5.957m → £2.068m; schools deficit: £5.233m
findings.quote: School balances have fallen year-on-year for a number of years and this downward trend is likely to continue, therefore it is considered appropriate to further protect schools budgets as far as possible in 2026/27, by not applying a top-slice from delegated schools budgets.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: Producer responsibility packaging (pEPR) funding is being cut by £1.931m (38.8%) in 2026/27, and the waste service is 'under pressure'
findings.detail: The council received £4.983m in pEPR funding for 2025/26 but this is confirmed to fall to £3.052m for 2026/27 — a reduction of £1.931m. This funding was being used for waste collection activity and to support recycling targets. The paper states: 'This significant reduction in year-on-year funding will inevitably put the waste service under pressure in 2026/27.' Additionally, the council's pEPR allocation was 'subject to a deduction adjustment for the Council not meeting the statutory municipal recycling rate in 2023/24.'
findings.matters: A major grant is being withdrawn, reducing expected income and creating service pressure. This is exogenous to the council's control and compounds waste service risk.
findings.quote: This significant reduction in year-on-year funding will inevitably put the waste service under pressure in 2026/27 with the funding in 2025/26 being used for waste collection activity and to assist the Council with achieving national recycling targets.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: The Strategic Transformation Programme contains £2m in unidentified cost reductions with explicit acknowledgment of execution risk
findings.detail: The budget includes a £2m assumption for cost reductions from the Strategic Transformation Programme, described as 'a combination of existing STP projects and new areas currently being worked up with an external partner.' The council explicitly warns: 'Clearly, including a general target is not without risk and will require Chief Officer project sponsors to prioritise and progress these projects in a timely manner. Robust arrangements will be put in place to monitor and report progress on the STP.' This hedging language indicates material uncertainty.
findings.matters: A budget balanced partly on unidentified savings represents budget risk. The hedging language ('robust arrangements will be put in place') indicates the council is aware savings are not yet locked in.
findings.figures: £2m STP target
findings.quote: Clearly, including a general target is not without risk and will require Chief Officer project sponsors to prioritise and progress these projects in a timely manner.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: Holiday pay claims (Brazel case) are underfunded, with 300+ live employment tribunal claims and only £0.254m held in reserves
findings.detail: Following the Supreme Court judgment in July 2022, there are currently 300+ live employment tribunal claims relating to holiday pay for part-time and term-time staff. The council holds £0.254m in reserves for this, but the paper explicitly warns: 'There is a risk that the final cost may be considerably more than the £0.254m currently held in reserves for this purpose.' The next preliminary hearing is 5 March 2026.
findings.matters: A contingent liability affecting 300+ staff claims that is acknowledged to be potentially vastly underfunded represents material financial risk. An adverse ruling could force significant reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: 300+ live claims; £0.254m reserved
findings.quote: There is a risk that the final cost may be considerably more than the £0.254m currently held in reserves for this purpose.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: £0.540m contingent liability from waste recycling infraction fines is pending Welsh Government discretion
findings.detail: The council did not meet statutory recycling targets in 2022/23 and 2023/24, exposing it to infraction fines of £0.356m and £0.184m respectively (total £0.540m). Welsh Government has deferred the decision on whether to levy these, pending the council's progress on a Resource & Waste Strategy action plan. The outcome remains uncertain.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability that could crystallise without the council's control, reducing available resources or requiring reserve drawdown.
findings.quote: The remaining infraction fine risk for 2022/23 and 2023/24 therefore is £0.540m. Officers continue to meet with Welsh Government to report on progress with the action plan.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: Out of county placements are projected to overspend by £1.831m in 2025/26, and the 2026/27 budget increase of £2m may still not be sufficient
findings.detail: The paper identifies out of county placements as 'an ongoing risk' with a projected 2025/26 overspend of £1.831m. The 2026/27 budget adds £2m (an 8.84% uplift on the 2025/26 base of £22.261m), but this follows a baseline budget that was already overspending. The council does not commit to this eliminating the risk.
findings.matters: An overspending budget line that requires sequential annual increases signals loss of control over a material cost category. The pattern suggests the budget is reactive rather than prospective.
findings.figures: £1.831m projected overspend in 2025/26; £2m uplift for 2026/27 on £22.261m base
findings.quote: The position on Out of County placements remains an ongoing risk and the projected overspend in the current financial year is £1.831m.

findings.paper_title: Council Fund Budget 2026/27 – Final Closing Stage
findings.headline: Social care demand is explicitly described as unsustainable and exceeding the council's capacity to respond
findings.detail: The council states: 'demand to support adults is already exceeding our capacity to respond to requests for assessments and once assessed, people may have to wait for care and support due to limited capacity within local authority and independent sector services.' A 20.82% increase in residents aged 65+ and 40.57% increase in those aged 80+ over the 2023-2034 period is driving this. The budget allocates a 13.98% increase for social care (£14.581m), but the council explicitly notes 'Social Services have limited options to deliver cost savings.'
findings.matters: A demand-led service that cannot be resource-constrained and is already at capacity represents an unfunded and open-ended liability. This is the council's largest risk exposure.
findings.figures: 13.98% social care budget increase; aged 65+ growing 20.82% (7,099 people); aged 80+ growing 40.57% (3,553 people)
findings.quote: The current position is therefore unsustainable, and Social Services have limited options to deliver cost savings.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, Treasury Management Policy Statement, Practices and Schedules 2026-2029.
findings.headline: Capital expenditure planned to increase, shifting the council's treasury focus toward more borrowing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The local context section identifies a planned increase in capital expenditure for 2026/27, which will require the council to shift its treasury activities from primarily investing funds to primarily borrowing to finance this expanded capital programme.
findings.matters: Growing capital expenditure signals either new service investment or major assets being acquired; either way, rising debt service costs will flow into revenue budgets, and lenders assess councils' ability to sustain this.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Activity in 2026/27 is expected to focus more on borrowing and less on investing as the Council's requirement to borrow is forecast to grow due to a planned increase in capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, Treasury Management Policy Statement, Practices and Schedules 2026-2029.
findings.headline: Council's long-term borrowing requirement forecast to grow significantly but amounts remain unconfirmed
findings.detail: The borrowing strategy indicates a significant long-term borrowing requirement, but specific amounts have not yet been confirmed. Until confirmed, the council will use short-term borrowing to bridge timing gaps. This creates uncertainty about the scale and timing of capital financing needs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what the council is actually planning to borrow and when, to assess debt capacity and financial risk. Unconfirmed amounts in February for a financial year starting in April is a compressed timeline.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The required amounts need to be confirmed before a commitment to long-term borrowing is made and the use of short-term borrowing will be used to assist during this period.

news_drafts.headline: £1.000m waste infrastructure capital deferred to 2027/28 pending completion of strategic review
news_drafts.lead: Material deferral of strategic infrastructure investment; finance director needs revised capital programme timeline; lender needs visibility on when waste capacity decisions and expenditure will occur to assess council's service provision capacity.

news_drafts.headline: HRA financing costs forecast to rise 290 basis points due to capital programme expansion
news_drafts.lead: Material 290bp year-on-year increase puts HRA leverage approaching typical prudential limits. Lender needs to assess whether HRA revenue base can sustain these elevated financing costs long-term and whether HRA business model remains viable.

news_drafts.headline: After over a decade of austerity, the council has exhausted most low-cost savings options and faces very difficult choices ahead
news_drafts.lead: This structural constraint means future budget gaps cannot be solved through incremental efficiency gains; they require material service cuts or tax increases
